title: Hierarchical Policy Learning via Spectral Decomposition
claim: Signals decompose in the frequency domain into a coarse, conditioning-driven component and a fine component conditioned on the coarse one.
layout: Top row left-to-right pipeline; two shaded panels below; color-coded low/high frequency
description: The top row runs left to right. A robot photo labeled Action Sequence goes through a DCT arrow into a spectral power plot. The plot is split into a green Low Freq region with large peaks and a pink High Freq region with small ripples. A Predict iDCT arrow then leads to a second robot photo. The bottom row has two shaded panels. The green panel on the left is Coarse Trajectory: a smooth teal sine wave over a robot photo with a red arc showing the motion path. Beneath it, the caption reads 'Low Freq depends on Language and Obs' with p(c^low | o_t, l). The pink panel on the right shows Fine Action, a rapid orange oscillation over a robot with jitter marks, and TeleOp Noise, a purple noisy signal over a robot photo with a human hand on a teleoperation device. Beneath it, the caption reads 'High Freq depends on Low Freq and Obs' with p(c^high | o_t, c^low). Green and pink color-code the two frequency bands throughout.
caption: Action sequences admit a coarse-to-fine structure in the spectral domain. CSP predicts low-frequency motion from observation and language, then generates high-frequency corrections conditioned on the coarse trajectory.
abstract: In this paper, we identify a semantic decomposition in robot action sequences, separating task-level motion intent from execution-level refinements. By analyzing actions in the spectral domain using the discrete cosine transform (DCT), we observe that low-frequency components capture global motion trajectories, while high-frequency components encode precise timing, alignment, and contact behaviors. Motivated by this structure, we propose Causal Spectral Policy (CSP), which models action generation as a causal coarse-to-fine process: coarse motion is predicted from observation and language, and fine corrections are generated conditionally on the realized trajectory. Across simulation and real-world evaluations, CSP consistently outperforms strong baselines on precision-sensitive manipulation tasks. Additionally, we propose human-inspired teleoperation noise injection as a data augmentation method, under which our approach demonstrates strong robustness to noisy demonstrations.
